questions.question: Describe the role of soldiers on the eastern frontier.
questions.expected_answer: British regiments defended the border, patrolled to recover cattle and fought the frontier wars; a line of forts was built (Grahamstown 1812 as HQ, Fort Willshire, Fort Beaufort, Fort Hare, later King William's Town); the Cape Regiment/Cape Mounted Riflemen of mainly Khoikhoi soldiers under British officers (skilled horsemen and marksmen, some rebelled in 1850); burgher commandos called up in wars; soldiers faced hard conditions.

questions.question: Explain how British frontier policy changed between about 1812 and 1854.
questions.expected_answer: Separation under Somerset: fixed border, forts, empty Ceded Territory, controlled trade (Fort Willshire fairs from 1824), 1817 agreement allowing recovery of cattle from any homestead. Treaty system from 1836 (Glenelg, Stockenstrom): Queen Adelaide Province returned, chiefs treated as independent rulers. Annexation after the War of the Axe: British Kaffraria under Harry Smith with British magistrates. Grey from 1854: 'civilising' policy - schools, hospitals, roads, salaried chiefs, labour, European (incl. German) settlement. Policies were inconsistent.

questions.question: Why did the 1820 Settlers come, and what was their impact?
questions.expected_answer: Push: unemployment and poverty in Britain after the Napoleonic Wars (1815); Parliament voted 50 000 pounds; about 90 000 applied, about 4000 chosen; free passage and 100 acres. Government aims: buffer on the frontier in the Zuurveld, more English-speakers. Landed at Algoa Bay (Port Elizabeth/Gqeberha) from April 1820; farms in Albany; early failure (inexperience, small farms, rust, 1823 floods). Impact: traders and craftsmen, growth of Grahamstown and Port Elizabeth, wool exports, press freedom (Pringle, Fairbairn, 1829), schools and churches; more pressure on Xhosa land and support for harsh policies (Godlonton), though some criticised injustice.
